comparison: Both evaluate negative control results (C65-C70) showing no effects on movement and motivation. OpenEval finds these controls strengthen timing specificity interpretation. Peer review finds them UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 2 explicitly requesting additional movement analysis (position tracking during intervals), suggesting the presented movement data is insufficient to rule out motor confounds.

Both address the main conclusion about complementary roles of D1/D2-MSNs (C17-C18). OpenEval finds it SUPPORTED by converging evidence from multiple experimental approaches. Peer review finds it UNCERTAIN due to concerns about statistical rigor, anatomical specificity of systemic drugs, and insufficient model validation, though Reviewer 3 notes consistency with previous research.

Both evaluate machine learning decoding results (C15-C16, C78-C81). OpenEval finds the naive Bayesian classifier approach appropriate with strong effect sizes. Peer review finds it UNCERTAIN, citing statistical concerns about sample size (cells vs. mice) and questioning anatomical specificity due to systemic drug delivery.

Both evaluate the drift-diffusion model (C6-C8, C97-C98). OpenEval finds it SUPPORTED with high R² values, though notes parameters were fit rather than derived from first principles. Peer review finds it UNCERTAIN, with editor and Reviewer 1 calling for stronger connection between model and experimental data, questioning validation of predictive power despite good fit.

Both evaluate optogenetically tagged neuron characterization (C38-C42). OpenEval finds tagging criteria appropriate with adequate sample sizes and proper statistical analysis. Peer review finds it SUPPORTED, with Reviewer 3 noting the approach is well-established, though Reviewer 1 mentions the dataset is relatively small.

Both evaluate pharmacological effects on neural dynamics (C13-C14, C71-C77). OpenEval finds neuron matching well-validated with appropriate statistics. Peer review finds it UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 2 questioning whether cells or mice were used for statistics, and Reviewer 3's systemic delivery concern undermining anatomical specificity.

Both evaluate interval timing task design and behavioral data (C2-C3, C27-C30, C82-C86). OpenEval finds the task well-described with appropriate controls and quantitative validation. Peer review finds it SUPPORTED as a well-established approach, though Reviewer 3 notes the task is better suited for elapsed time perception rather than interval timing per se.

Both evaluate PCA analysis of opposing dynamics (C47-C52). OpenEval finds robust statistical support with appropriate mixed-effects models and significant variance explained. Peer review finds it UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 2 critically challenging the statistical approach (using number of cells vs. mice for tests) and Reviewer 1 calling for more rigorous characterization despite visually apparent dynamics.

Both evaluate D2 receptor blockade effects (C11, C61-C62). OpenEval finds results consistent with optogenetic findings despite systemic delivery limitations. Peer review finds it UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 3 explicitly stating systemic delivery makes it difficult to conclude effects are specific to dorsomedial striatum and recommending local infusion.

Both evaluate D1 receptor blockade effects (C12, C63-C64). OpenEval finds results consistent with optogenetic findings with within-subject controls. Peer review finds it UNCERTAIN for the same reason as D2 blockade: Reviewer 3's concern that systemic delivery prevents conclusions about dorsomedial striatum specificity.

Both evaluate optogenetic manipulation of D2-MSNs (C9, C55-C57). OpenEval finds causal effects well-demonstrated with appropriate controls and large effect sizes. Peer review finds it UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 2 questioning whether behavioral effects reflect timing deficits or motor impairment, requesting position tracking analysis to clarify mechanism.

Both evaluate optogenetic manipulation of D1-MSNs (C10, C58-C60). OpenEval finds causal effects demonstrated with appropriate controls supporting complementary roles. Peer review finds it UNCERTAIN for same reason as D2-MSN manipulation: Reviewer 2's concern about whether increased response times reflect timing-specific vs. motor deficits.

Partial overlap on opposing dynamics claims (C43-C46). OpenEval R2 evaluates these as part of converging evidence for opposing dynamics with appropriate optogenetic tagging. Peer R1 includes these claims in broader UNCERTAIN evaluation, questioning statistical validity (cells vs. mice) despite visually apparent patterns.

Both address trial-by-trial GLM analysis (C53-C54). OpenEval finds it provides complementary evidence with appropriate controls for movement. Peer review includes these claims in broader UNCERTAIN evaluation of opposing dynamics, with statistical approach concerns and call for more rigorous characterization.

OpenEval R14 evaluates background and motivation claims (C1, C19-C26) as SUPPORTED with appropriate citations and clear articulation of knowledge gap. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these introductory claims.

OpenEval R15 evaluates prior findings summary (C31-C33) as SUPPORTED with appropriate citations establishing foundation for current study. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these background claims.

OpenEval R16 evaluates anatomical descriptions (C92-C93) as SUPPORTED, noting these are well-established facts about basal ganglia circuitry. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these anatomical background claims.

OpenEval R17 evaluates comprehensive methodological details (C99-C119) as SUPPORTED, noting ethical approval, appropriate statistical methods, and data availability. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing these methodological claims, though reviewers raised concerns about statistical approaches in results sections.
Peer R1 also includes claims C4-C5 which do not appear in any OpenEval result. These may relate to additional aspects of the opposing dynamics findings that OpenEval did not separately evaluate.
